headline: First Circuit weighs Rhode Island arts group’s challenge to NEA funding restrictions
dek: The appeal asks whether the federal arts agency may disadvantage grant applications it views as promoting ‘gender ideology’ after a Rhode Island judge found the policy violated the First Amendment and administrative law.
body: A Rhode Island-led challenge to the federal government’s rules for arts grants reached the First Circuit Court of Appeals on Wednesday, putting a Providence-based cultural organization at the center of a broader dispute over whether agencies may condition public funding on a project’s viewpoint. The court’s [official oral-argument record](https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/doar/search-results) lists Rhode Island Latino Arts v. National Endowment for the Arts as case 25-2113, argued Oct. 7 in Boston.

The appeal concerns the National Endowment for the Arts’ response to an executive order directing federal agencies to ensure that federal funds are not used to promote what the order calls “gender ideology.” The NEA initially required applicants to acknowledge that condition. After the organizations sued, the agency withdrew that first version and later adopted a process under which its chairperson could consider whether a proposed project promoted gender ideology when making the final funding decision. The policy said that factor would not be the sole reason to deny an application, but it could count against approval and could not count in the project’s favor, according to the [Rhode Island federal district court’s decision](https://www.riaclu.org/app/uploads/2025/03/Decision-%E2%80%93-RILA-v.-NEA-1.pdf).

U.S. District Judge William E. Smith ruled in September 2025 that the final policy violated the First Amendment because it treated NEA-funded art as private speech and assigned negative weight to a viewpoint about gender identity. He also ruled that the policy violated the Administrative Procedure Act, finding that the agency had not adequately explained its decision or tied the restriction to the criteria Congress gave the NEA. The order enjoined the government from applying the viewpoint-based standard to the plaintiffs and vacated the plan. The court rejected the plaintiffs’ separate Fifth Amendment claim, so the ruling was only partly in their favor.

Rhode Island Latino Arts is a statewide nonprofit based in Providence and Central Falls that promotes and preserves Latino art, history and culture. Its programs include artists’ networks, public art, oral histories and community events. The group joined the case with National Queer Theater, The Theater Offensive and Theatre Communications Group. In a [statement released after the hearing](https://www.riaclu.org/news/first-circuit-hears-arguments-in-case-challenging-viewpoint-based-penalties-in-federal-funding-for-the-arts/), RILA executive director Marta V. Martínez said artists should not have to choose between access to public funding and telling their stories fully. That is the plaintiffs’ position, not a finding by the appeals court.

The federal government is defending a different understanding of the grant program. The ACLU of Rhode Island said the government argues that its funding decisions are government speech and that considering viewpoints is consistent with the law establishing the NEA. A case summary from the [Institute for Free Speech](https://www.ifs.org/podcast/free-speech-arguments-episode-55-can-the-government-withhold-arts-funding-based-on-viewpoint/) describes the government’s appeal as raising three questions: whether the district court misapplied the Administrative Procedure Act, whether the policy is facially unconstitutional and whether the remedy was too broad. Those arguments remain contested; the First Circuit has not ruled on them.

The dispute matters beyond one grant cycle because the NEA is a national funding agency, while Rhode Island Latino Arts is a local organization whose work connects artists with schools, libraries, museums and community spaces. The lower court’s reasoning says the government may support private expression without turning the funded work into the government’s own message, but it may not then downgrade applications because officials disfavor a viewpoint. The government’s position would give the agency more room to treat the message of a proposed project as part of its funding judgment.

The First Circuit’s decision could clarify how First Amendment and administrative-law limits apply when federal agencies distribute competitive grants. The ACLU of Rhode Island said the ruling could affect funding restrictions in areas beyond the arts, while the case record shows that the panel is also considering the statutory and remedial questions separately from the constitutional issue. Wednesday’s argument produced no immediate decision. The court will issue its ruling later, and the parties’ filings and the district court injunction—not campaign statements or predictions about the outcome—will determine what happens to the challenged policy in the meantime.
